lesson.title: Samples and populations

steps.headline: Who you want to know about, and who you ask

lead.text: Start with the question the shop owner is trying to answer: how much do her customers spend on a visit? The customers she cares about are all of them, everyone who shops there. Statisticians call that whole group the population. The word doesn't have to mean people. It could be the homes in a town, the bolts made in a factory this week or the trees in a wood. The population is whatever group the question is about.

Measuring a whole population is often too slow or too expensive. Suppose a council wants to know how many of a town's 8,000 homes have damp. Visiting every door would take months, so it visits 300 homes and counts the damp ones there. Those 300 homes are a sample, the part of the population that actually gets measured.

A sample stands in for the population. You measure the few and hope that what you find holds for everyone. Whether that hope is justified depends on how the sample was picked, and the rest of this lesson follows that question. First, a quick check on the two words.
Try the same split on a different survey. Decide which number describes the part that is measured.

Now back to the shop. The owner has two kinds of customer. Six come in the morning for a coffee and a paper, and each spends £2. Six come in the evening for the week's shopping, and each spends £8. Every one of them is part of the population she wants to describe, because her question is about all her customers, including the ones she never met that morning.

On the morning of her survey she asked the morning shoppers only. Those six are her sample. The evening shoppers are still in the population, even though nobody asked them anything. The picture shows the shop, with the people who were asked marked out. Switch between the samples to see who each one reaches.

afterFigure.text: The population stays fixed while the sample changes. Choose a different group of people to ask and you have a different sample, but the same customers remain the population. That makes it worth counting exactly who is in the population before doing anything with it.

lead.text: The owner asked the morning shoppers only. Think about who her question is really about, then count them.

reveal.text: The evening shoppers weren't asked, and they still belong to the population.

steps.headline: The average of a whole population

lead.text: The owner's question is about an average, so the next job is to find the average spend of the whole population. You already know how: add up every value and divide by how many there are. When the values come from the whole population, the result is called the population mean. The same sum done on a sample gives the sample mean.

Values that repeat make the adding shorter. Take a stall with four customers, three who spend £1 and one who spends £5. Adding all four gives 1 + 1 + 1 + 5 = 8, and 8 ÷ 4 = 2, so the population mean is £2. Gathering up the repeats gives the same total as 3 × 1 + 1 × 5.

The count you divide by has to include everyone in the population, whichever group they belong to. A sample mean uses only the people who were asked. The two can differ, and the gap between them is what the rest of this lesson is about.

steps.headline: Five customers spend £2 and five spend £6. Find the population mean.

workedSteps.text: Count every member of the population.
Divide the total by the members.

steps.headline: Find the mean spend of the shop's whole population.

lead.text: The shop has six customers who spend £2 and six who spend £8. Count them, add up what they spend and divide.

Put the two answers side by side. Asking the morning shoppers only, the owner found an average spend of £2. The population mean is £5. Her sample mean is far from it, though nobody misreported and she added correctly. Every morning shopper told her the truth.

The reason lies in how the sample was chosen. Standing at the till in the morning gave the evening shoppers no chance of being asked. A sample whose method leaves part of the population out is called a biased sample, because its answer is pushed in one direction, here towards the low spenders. Asking more morning shoppers would only repeat £2 more times. A bigger sample from the same method carries the same bias.

A better sample mirrors the population. This population is half morning shoppers and half evening shoppers, so a sample with equal numbers from each group should land close to the population mean. You can test that on the next screen.
Take a sample with three customers from each group. Work out its sample mean and compare it with the population mean you found.

reveal.text: A sample that mirrors the population reached the population mean here.

lead.text: The balanced sample hit the population mean exactly, but it had an advantage. We knew the two groups in advance and built the sample to match. The owner usually doesn't know the groups, and a sample picked by hand tends to lean towards the people who are easy to ask.

The usual remedy is to let chance do the picking. Suppose she wrote every customer's name on a card, shuffled the cards and drew some. Every customer would have a known chance of being asked, and nobody would have a chance of zero. A sample chosen like that is a probability sample. The chances don't have to be equal. What matters is that they are known and that every member has some chance, so the method itself can't shut a group out.

Chance doesn't promise a perfect result. One probability sample can still land away from the population mean through plain luck, and one match in a made-up example, like our balanced sample, shows only that it worked there. What chance removes is the systematic lean. It also explains why a very large sample isn't a cure by itself: if the method excludes a group, more answers just repeat the same lean.

A shop down the road has six customers who spend £4 and six who spend £10. A survey that reached only one group would miss the other. Find the population mean, the figure a good sample is trying to reach.

reveal.text: You found the target a sample is aiming for. Define who you want to learn about before deciding whom to measure.

lesson.orientation: Identify a population, compare selection methods and explain why a large biased sample can still mislead.
lesson.nextAction: Try a new case and return for recall after a delay.

blocks.text: A shop owner wants to know how much her customers spend on a visit. She has no time to ask all of them, so one morning she stands by the till and asks everyone who comes in. By lunchtime she has a tidy list of answers and an average she feels sure about.

What she doesn't know is that her shop has two kinds of customer. Those who come in the morning pick up a coffee and a paper and spend very little. The ones who come in the evening do the week's shopping and spend a good deal more. Her list describes only the first kind, and she would have got much the same average from a thousand morning customers as from six.

Her arithmetic is fine. The trouble lies in who she asked, and this lesson follows her survey from the question she wanted answered to the answer she got, then looks at how she should have chosen. The same issue sits behind every poll and product survey you will come across.

intro.promise: By the end you'll tell a population from a sample, and say why a large sample can still mislead.

recap.keyIdea: A sample is only the part you measure. If the method leaves part of the population out, a large sample still misleads.

blocks.text: You followed the owner's survey from her question to her answer. Asking the morning shoppers gave a mean of £2, the whole population's mean was £5, and a sample with three from each group gave £5 again. Choosing by chance is the way to avoid leaving a group out.

recap.nextHook: This is the last lesson of the course. Chance, centres, spread and samples are what most reports of data are built on, and the next time a headline quotes an average, the first thing to ask is who was asked.

questions.prompt: The shop's customers are six morning shoppers and six evening shoppers, and the owner asked only the morning ones. How many members does her population have?
hints: Who is her question about: only the people she asked, or all her customers?
The evening shoppers belong to the population even though nobody asked them.
Add the morning group's size to the evening group's size.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The population contains six morning and six evening members: 6 + 6 = 12.

questions.onCorrect: 12. The population includes everyone, checked or not.

misconceptions.feedback: That is one group, the people she asked. The population has both groups.

questions.prompt: The shop has six customers who spend £2 and six who spend £8. What is the population mean, in pounds?
hints: Use every member of the population.
Count each of the two group values six times.
Use (6 × 2 + 6 × 8) divided by the total number of members.
questions.onCorrect: 5. Total of 60 over 12 members, using everyone.

misconceptions.feedback: That adds the two group values. Each counts once for every member.
That is the morning group alone. The population has both.

questions.prompt: A sample matches the population mean in one constructed example. What follows?
hints: One observed match cannot establish a general guarantee.

acceptedIdeas: It shows agreement here, without guaranteeing agreement elsewhere
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Agreement in this constructed sample is evidence about this case only. It does not guarantee that another sample or another measured quantity will agree.

choices.label: It proves the method is unbiased in every population
It shows agreement here, without guaranteeing agreement elsewhere
It proves there is no sampling error

questions.onCorrect: One match shows agreement here. It does not guarantee agreement elsewhere.

misconceptions.feedback: One match in a made-up example cannot prove a method works in every population.
Sampling error is the chance gap between a sample and the population. One match does not remove it.

questions.prompt: A shop down the road has six customers who spend £4 and six who spend £10. What is the population mean, in pounds?
hints: The two groups have equal size.
The group sizes are equal, so both contribute the same weight.
Use (6 × 4 + 6 × 10) divided by the combined group count.
questions.onCorrect: 7. The groups are equal in size, so the mean sits midway between the values.

misconceptions.feedback: That adds the two group values. Each counts for every member of its group.
That is the morning group alone. The population has both.

questions.prompt: A survey meant for a whole city reaches only weekday visitors to one gym. What is the main limitation?
hints: Compare the target population with the people the survey can reach.

acceptedIdeas: Other parts of the target population are systematically excluded
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The sampling frame omits people who do not visit that gym on weekdays. Increasing responses within that frame does not remove the systematic exclusion.

choices.label: Other parts of the target population are systematically excluded
Every city resident has the same inclusion chance

questions.onCorrect: The method leaves out other parts of the city, and more replies would not fix that.

misconceptions.feedback: Asking many people is not the problem. Ask who could never be asked.
Not every resident can be reached through one gym on weekdays.

questions.prompt: Which description fits a probability sample?
hints: Known inclusion probabilities do not have to be equal.

acceptedIdeas: Selection by chance with known, nonzero inclusion probabilities
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: A probability sample uses chance selection with known, nonzero inclusion probabilities. Those probabilities can differ between units; equal probabilities are a special case.

choices.label: Selection by chance with known, nonzero inclusion probabilities

questions.onCorrect: Chance selection with known, non-zero chances of inclusion makes a probability sample.

misconceptions.feedback: Speed is not the test. A probability sample is chosen by chance.
Volunteers choose themselves. A probability sample uses chance with known probabilities.

questions.prompt: A shop has 12 customers. Six are morning shoppers who each spend £2. Six are evening shoppers who each spend £8. You ask only the morning shoppers. What average spend do you find?
hints: Who does your survey reach?
Every morning shopper spends the same amount.
The average of identical amounts is that amount.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: All six morning shoppers spend £2, so the average is £2.

questions.onCorrect: £2. The survey was honest and still missed half the customers.

misconceptions.feedback: That would be the average of every customer. Your survey only reaches the morning shoppers.
That is the evening shoppers. They were not asked.

questions.prompt: A town has 5,000 homes and a survey asks 200 of them. How many homes are in the sample?
hints: Which homes were actually asked?
Is the sample the whole town or part of it?
Count the homes that were asked.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The sample is the 200 homes that were asked.

questions.onCorrect: 200. The sample is the part you measure; the 5,000 homes are the population.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the population, everyone you want to learn about. The sample is the part you measure.

questions.prompt: Why count both groups when finding the population mean?
hints: Who does the population include?

acceptedIdeas: The population is everyone you want to learn about
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The population is the whole target set, so every member of both groups belongs in it.

choices.label: The population is everyone you want to learn about
The larger group always counts more

questions.onCorrect: The population is everyone you want to learn about, so both groups count.

misconceptions.feedback: Here the groups are the same size. The population is defined by who you want to learn about.
This is about the population, not the sample. A sample need not be balanced.

questions.prompt: Six customers spend £2 and six spend £8. What is the total spend of all of them, in pounds?
hints: Six members are worth the first amount each.
Find six lots of each value, then add.
Add six times the first value to six times the second.
questions.onCorrect: 60. Count each group value once per member.

misconceptions.feedback: That adds the two group values. Each is counted once for every member.

questions.prompt: A balanced sample takes three customers from each group, who spend £2 and £8. What is the sample mean, in pounds?
hints: Add the six sampled values.
Three lots of the first value plus three lots of the second.
Divide the total by the six members sampled.
questions.onCorrect: 5. Half from each group balances out to the middle.

misconceptions.feedback: That adds the two group values. Each is counted three times.
That is the total. Divide by the six members sampled.

questions.prompt: A population has four members worth 3 and four worth 9. What is its mean?
hints: Use every member of the population.
Four lots of each value, added.
Divide the total by the number of members.
questions.onCorrect: 6. Total over members, using the whole population.

misconceptions.feedback: That adds the two group values. Each counts for every member of its group.
That is one group alone. The population has both.

A population is the full target set; a sample is a subset of it that is measured.

Six 2s and six 8s total 60 over 12 members: 5.
